about.intro: Nearly a decade of crafting software that scales.
paragraphs: I'm a Solution Architect who keeps both eyes on the machine and the room. From AAA mobile titles at Gameloft to AI-powered recruitment at Paradox, I've designed platforms that handle millions of requests and led the teams that own them long after the diagrams are filed away.

My work tends to live at the intersection of system design and team design — drawing the architecture, writing the playbooks, and coaching the engineers who'll inherit it. Good systems aren't shipped, they're inherited; I optimize for the engineer reading this code on a bad Wednesday.

These days I'm building my own products — writing essays at duthaho.dev, shipping open-source AI tooling, and treating every codebase as a teaching artifact. The strongest architectures, in my experience, emerge from understanding both the code and the people who write it.

articles.title: We picked Redis Streams over Kafka: and what the docs don't tell you upfront
articles.excerpt: Two services needed to talk to each other, and the team's first reflex was "just stand up Kafka, do it properly." But we had no Kafka, nobody had ever run it, and Redis was already in the stack. This is the story of choosing Redis Streams in the spirit of YAGNI — and an honest accounting of the costs the marketing docs never mention: everything lives in RAM, eviction wipes whole streams, failover can eat acked writes, and the day I knew we'd have to go back to Kafka.

articles.title: A rate limiter isn't an algorithm-picking problem: an interview that just kept digging deeper
articles.excerpt: I walked into an architect interview and got asked to "design a rate limiter." I started reciting algorithm names — and realized the interviewer didn't care which one I picked. Every answer only opened a deeper question: with twenty servers, where does the count live; whose clock do you trust; if Redis dies, do you let requests through or block them; and finally — is rate limiting even the whole story. The algorithm is the ten-minute answer; the rest of it was the interview.

articles.title: Redis never gives you anything for free: the hidden price behind every layer of cache
articles.excerpt: When I started out, caching meant one thing to me: "API slow? Throw Redis at it." Cramming for an architect interview, I finally saw what that "throw it in" really dragged along — invalidation, three distinct ways to crush a database, cache–DB consistency — and that it was really the Dual Write Problem wearing a disguise. Caching is never free; every layer of cache is a line of debt against consistency.

articles.title: From monolith to idempotency:: one thread, not six flashcards
articles.excerpt: Prepping for an architect interview, I realized leveling up isn't about writing better code — it's about seeing the whole system. Six topics I'd once memorized by rote — microservices, 2PC, Saga, CAP, Outbox, idempotency — turned out to be a single causal thread: each solution births the next problem.

articles.title: Two workers: inside the AI machine
articles.excerpt: Every time an AI answers, two workers with opposite temperaments take turns at the bench — and nearly every trick for speeding up inference is born from the tension between them. A trip inside the reasoning machine: prefill, decode, KV cache, batching, quantization, and why the day eventually comes to run your own servers.
